ui.title: The spark in a neuron
ui.lede: Every thought, twitch and touch rides on a tiny electric pulse. Poke a nerve cell, watch the ions rush through their gates, and see the real protein that lets only potassium through.
ui.modelNote: The pulse is computed as you watch with the Hodgkin and Huxley equations from 1952, worked out on the giant nerve fibre of a squid. It is the classic model, not a human neuron, so its numbers are close to textbook human values but not the same.
ui.labIntro: This is a slice of the cell membrane. The outside of the cell is on top, the inside below. Pick a strength, press Stimulate, and watch the voltage trace and the gates.
ui.membraneLabel: Membrane slice with sodium and potassium ions, the sodium potassium pump, a voltage gated sodium channel, a voltage gated potassium channel and a potassium leak channel
ui.traceLabel: Voltage trace: membrane voltage in millivolts over the last 30 milliseconds, with how open the sodium and potassium channels are
ui.strengthHelp: How hard the 1 millisecond push of current is. Try weak and strong.
ui.thresholdHint: In this model a 1 ms push fires a spike from about {v} µA/cm² up.
ui.speedNote: 1 second here is {ms} ms in the cell

ui.saidNoSpike: No spike. The voltage only reached {peak} mV, below threshold, and slid back to rest.
ui.saidRefractory: No new spike. The sodium channels were still locked shut from the last one. Wait a few milliseconds and try again.
ui.tryTwice: Try this: press Stimulate twice, fast. The second push does nothing while the sodium gates are locked.
ui.gatesTitle: The three gates inside the model
ui.gateH: h: Na+ inactivation gate (shuts a bit later)
ui.gatesNote: Na+ current flows when all three m gates are open and h is still open. K+ current needs four n gates open. That is why the K+ channels lag behind.
ui.phasesIntro: The panel above follows the live model. Here is every step in order, so you can read it at your own pace.
ui.restIntro: Rest is not resting. Pumps have packed K+ inside and pushed Na+ outside. Each ion feels two pushes: its concentration difference, and the voltage. The Nernst equation finds the voltage where those two cancel for one ion.

ui.raceIntro: A spike does not stay put. It sets off the patch of membrane next to it, which sets off the next, all the way down the axon. Wrapping the axon in fatty myelin lets the signal leap from gap to gap.

phases.name: Resting
phases.text: At rest the inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside: -65 mV in this squid model, about -70 mV in a typical textbook neuron, and anywhere from -60 to -80 mV depending on the cell. Leak K+ channels are always a little open, so K+ slowly seeps out and holds the voltage near its balance point. The sodium potassium pump keeps the ion differences topped up.

phases.name: Pushed
phases.short: A small push makes the inside less negative.
phases.text: A stimulus pushes positive charge in and the voltage rises. This is called depolarization. If the push is too small, nothing big happens: the leak channels pull the voltage straight back to rest. That is a below threshold bump.

phases.name: Rising
phases.short: Na+ gates fly open. Na+ rushes in.
phases.text: Once the voltage passes threshold (about -55 mV in textbook neurons), voltage gated Na+ channels open. Na+ is about 12 times more concentrated outside and is pulled toward the negative inside, so it floods in. In the model you can see it snowball: every bit of rise opens more Na+ gates, which lets in more Na+. The inside flips positive in well under a millisecond.

phases.name: Peak
phases.text: The voltage tops out near +30 to +40 mV. In the model it stops short of the Na+ balance point (+50 mV here), because the Na+ inactivation gates are already shutting and the K+ channels are starting to open. Every spike in the same cell peaks at about the same height, however hard you pushed.

phases.name: Falling
phases.short: Na+ gates lock. K+ flows out.
phases.text: The Na+ channel's second gate, the inactivation gate, plugs the pore a fraction of a millisecond after it opened. Meanwhile the slower voltage gated K+ channels open. K+ is about 39 times more concentrated inside, so it rushes out and carries positive charge with it. The voltage drops back down. This is repolarization.

phases.name: Undershoot
phases.short: Too far: a dip below rest.
phases.text: The K+ channels are slow to close, so K+ keeps leaving for a moment and the inside dips below rest, by about 5 to 10 mV. This dip is called hyperpolarization or the undershoot. Then the K+ channels close and the leak channels bring the voltage back to rest.

phases.name: Refractory
phases.text: Right after a spike, a new one cannot start, whatever the push: the Na+ inactivation gates are still shut. This is the absolute refractory period. A little later, once those gates reset, a new spike can start, but only with a bigger push than before: the relative refractory period. Try it in the panel: press Stimulate twice, fast.

phases.name: Topping up
phases.short: The pump keeps the gradients ready.
phases.text: Each spike moves only a tiny fraction of the ions, so a nerve cell can fire hundreds of times in a row without running down. Over the longer run, the sodium potassium pump spends one ATP to throw 3 Na+ out and bring 2 K+ in. About a quarter of the energy cells use goes into making and keeping these voltages.

pump.text: Na+/K+ pump: uses one ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, against their gradients. Always running, slowly. Drawn slowed down.

naChan.text: Voltage gated Na+ channel: an activation gate that opens at threshold and an inactivation gate that plugs it shortly after.

kChan.text: Voltage gated K+ channel: one gate, opens more slowly than the Na+ channel and closes late.

leak.text: K+ leak channel: always slightly open. It sets the resting voltage.

fibres.extra: Across the whole nervous system, myelinated axons reach up to 150 m/s and bare ones typically 0.5 to 10 m/s. Wider axons are faster too, like water in a wide river compared with a narrow creek.

how.t: In water, a K+ ion wears a shell of water molecules. To enter the filter it has to shed that shell. The filter's oxygen atoms are spaced just right to stand in for the water, so K+ slips through easily.
Na+ is smaller. It cannot touch all those oxygens at once, so it keeps its water shell and stays out. Only about 1 Na+ gets through for every 10,000 K+.
The oxygens come from the protein's own backbone, from the K+ channel signature sequence, which reads TVGYG in this file. The filter is only about 12 Å long. Below it is a wider, water filled cavity.
K+ ions line up single file in the filter. They push on each other, and that push helps them keep moving through instead of getting stuck.
KcsA comes from a bacterium, but its sequence is like that of all known K+ channels, most of all in the pore. So its shape shows the basic rules of how K+ channels pick K+.

keyIdeas.t: A neuron at rest is like a charged battery: pumps keep Na+ outside and K+ inside, and leaky K+ channels make the inside about 70 mV negative.
An action potential is all or none. A push below threshold fades away. A push past threshold gives a full spike of the same height every time.
The spike is two kinds of gates taking turns: fast Na+ channels let Na+ rush in and flip the inside positive, then slower K+ channels let K+ out to bring it back.
After each spike the Na+ channels are locked for a moment, the refractory period. A second push in that window does nothing, and a bit later only a stronger push works.
Myelin makes signals leap from gap to gap. Myelinated fibres carry signals at up to about 120 m/s, while thin bare fibres manage about 2 m/s.

misconceptions.myth: A stronger stimulus makes a bigger spike.
misconceptions.truth: Spikes are all or none and peak at about the same voltage. A stronger stimulus makes more spikes, closer together, not bigger ones.

misconceptions.myth: Nerve signals are electricity racing down a wire at nearly the speed of light.
misconceptions.truth: The spike is rebuilt by ion channels patch by patch. Even the fastest nerves top out around 150 m/s, and bare ones crawl at about 1 m/s.

misconceptions.myth: During a spike the cell swaps all its sodium and potassium.
misconceptions.truth: Only a tiny fraction of the ions cross. A neuron can fire hundreds of times before the pumps need to catch up.

misconceptions.myth: The sodium potassium pump is what makes the spike happen.
misconceptions.truth: The spike comes from voltage gated channels letting ions flow downhill. The pump works slowly in the background, keeping the gradients ready.

misconceptions.myth: Potassium channels let any small ion through, so sodium should slip through even more easily.
misconceptions.truth: Na+ is smaller but cannot fit the filter's ring of oxygens, so it keeps its water shell and stays out. About 1 Na+ passes per 10,000 K+.

vocab.definition: The voltage across a cell membrane, inside compared with outside, measured in millivolts (mV).
The steady negative voltage of a neuron that is not signalling, about -70 mV in a typical neuron.
A quick all or none flip of the membrane voltage from negative to positive and back, the signal neurons use.
The voltage a stimulus must reach for voltage gated Na+ channels to open and a spike to start, about -55 mV in textbook neurons.
A change that makes the inside of the cell less negative, moving the voltage toward zero.
The return of the voltage toward rest after the peak of a spike, driven by K+ leaving the cell.
A dip below the resting voltage, as at the end of a spike while K+ channels are still open.
The short time after a spike when a new spike cannot start (absolute) or needs a stronger push (relative).
An ion channel that opens or closes when the membrane voltage changes.
A membrane protein that uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, keeping the ion gradients in place.
The narrowest part of an ion channel pore, which picks the ion that may pass. In K+ channels it is lined by backbone oxygen atoms.
A fatty insulating wrap around an axon, laid down in bands, that speeds up signals.
A bare gap between myelin bands, crowded with voltage gated channels that regenerate the spike.
The way a spike jumps from node to node along a myelinated axon (from Latin saltare, to leap).
The formula for the voltage at which one ion's concentration push and electrical pull cancel out.
